printed_headline_estimate: Table 4 (p. 13 / PDF p. 10), OLS regression on village Sanitation availability CFA index (N = 249 rural villages, R2 = 0.419): Governance — Elderly People's Association (dummy): b = 0.609*** (SE = 0.116, p < 0.01); Cadre service time (years): b = 0.001 (SE = 0.006, p >= 0.10). Primary investor of village infrastructure (ref: Collective economy) — Residents + others: printed 0.342*** (SE = 0.113, p < 0.01; true direction is negative [-0.342***], as text on p. 14 / PDF p. 11 states villages relying solely on individuals 'fared much worse' than collective-economy villages, reflecting dropped minus signs in Wiley Tables 3-4); Government: printed 0.070 (SE = 0.127, p >= 0.10).
publication_year_note: Published in Asia & the Pacific Policy Studies, vol. 5, no. 1, pp. 4-17, January 2018 (copyright 2018; Received 24 October 2017, Revised 23 November 2017, Accepted 27 November 2017).
rationale: Full text (14 pages) empirically estimates a multivariable OLS regression (Table 4, p. 13 / PDF p. 10; N = 249 rural villages from CHARLS 2011, R2 = 0.419) of a community sanitation availability CFA index (combining village sewer system, waste collection, public toilets and improved public toilets/sewer system; Criterion 4) on village governance arrangements and infrastructure financing/ownership regimes, controlling for village population, migration, age structure, per capita income, collective investment and land area. Under village governance (Family A: governance-arrangement; also touching Family B participatory self-governance), having an Elderly People's Association—recognised since 1982 as an autonomous village self-governance body influencing cadre decisions—is significantly positively associated with village sanitation availability (b = 0.609***, SE = 0.116, p < 0.01), whereas elected cadre tenure under the Organic Law of Village Committees is null (b = 0.001, SE = 0.006). Under infrastructure financing/provisioning structure (also eligible under Family C: collective vs state vs individual investor regime following the 2000/2004 public finance reforms), reliance on residents/individuals rather than the collective economy significantly worsens sanitation availability (printed 0.342***, SE = 0.113, p < 0.01; true sign negative per p. 14 text and dropped minus signs in Tables 3-4).
